description: Behavioral evals for the agent's use of the background-process surface. The two tools under test (both in horizon/tools/processes/): (a) `process(action='spawn', command=...)` spawns a long-running command into a session-scoped registry and returns `{session_id, pid, status: 'running'}` immediately (this is where `bash`'s former `background=True` moved); a foreground `bash` command that exceeds `timeout_s` auto-promotes into the same registry rather than getting killed — this is now fixed internal behavior, not a model-facing `on_timeout` choice. (b) `process(action=...)` drives the lifecycle — `list`, `poll`, `log`, `wait`, `kill`, `write`. The behaviors these evals pin: (1) the model picks `process(action='spawn')` for commands it knows will outlive a single turn (dev servers, long builds, watching for an event); (2) when a command times out it follows up with `process(action='wait')` or `process(action='kill')` instead of giving up; (3) when a foreground command hangs on an interactive prompt, the model recovers via either re-running with non-interactive flags (-y, --yes) OR writing to stdin via `process(action='write')`. NOTE: project eval_config.json grades against rubric_based_final_response_quality_v1 only — tool selection is encoded in rubric text, not via a trajectory grader.

parts.text: Start the dev server with `npm run dev` and keep it running while you check that it's serving on port 3000.

property.description: The response invokes `process(action='spawn', command='npm run dev')` (NOT a default foreground `bash` call) for `npm run dev`. A dev server is the textbook background case — it runs forever, blocking the turn would never return. A response that calls `bash` foreground and waits for it to exit fails this rubric.

After spawning the background session, the response inspects it via the `process` tool (e.g. `process(action='poll')` to see boot output, or `process(action='log')`) instead of just claiming the server started. Reporting success without checking is the failure mode this rubric guards against.

Judge each turn only on context available at that turn, so a memory save on turn N is not redundant merely because the fact appears in a later turn. Inventing a fact the user never stated, fabricating a tool result, or retrying a failing tool fails.

The response is useful given the real constraints of the turn. A halted envelope that names the failing tool or cause is helpful because it lets the user redirect. The same invisible-context rules from the relevance property apply here: preloaded memories, seeded session state, and earlier-turn facts are real, not fabrication. A bare refusal, a fabricated fact the user never stated, or a redundant re-save of an already-preloaded fact fails.

parts.text: Run the full test suite with `pytest tests/` and tell me the result. It usually takes about 3 minutes.

property.description: When `bash` returns `{timed_out: true, status: 'running', session_id: ...}` (auto-promotion), the response follows up by calling `process(action='wait', session_id=...)` (or repeated `process(action='poll', ...)`) on the returned session_id rather than giving up, reporting failure, or re-running the command from scratch. The whole point of auto-promotion is that the agent can keep watching — not following up wastes the partial progress.

The response does NOT call `process(action='kill', ...)` on the test-run session unless the user asks to stop it. The user wanted the result; killing aborts the run and loses progress. Killing is appropriate for runaway commands or when the user changes their mind — neither applies here.

If the agent's first attempt at installing ripgrep returns an interactive-prompt signal (the runtime detects a `[Y/n]` or `password:` wait and either auto-promotes or returns an `interactive: true` hint), the response recovers — either by re-running with `-y`/`--yes`/`--assume-yes`, or by using `process(action='write', data='y')` against the registered session. A response that gives up after the first prompt-stuck call, or re-runs the same interactive command without changing it, fails.

When both options are available, the response prefers the non-interactive flag (`-y`) over `process(action='write')`. Re-running with `-y` is idempotent and side-effect-free; writing `y` to stdin works but is brittle if the prompt copy changes. A response that immediately reaches for `process(write)` without trying the flag is technically OK but less robust — only the worst pattern (giving up entirely) fully fails this rubric.

This rubric catches over-eager use of the background surface.
